subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun in our Solar System?
questions.explain: Mercury is the innermost planet, orbiting closest to the Sun.

questions.q: What holds the planets in their orbits around the Sun?
options: The gravitational force of the Sun
The magnetic field of the Sun
questions.explain: Gravity from the Sun provides the force that keeps the planets in orbit.

questions.q: Stars form from a large cloud of which materials pulled together by gravity?
questions.explain: A star begins as a cloud of dust and gas (a nebula) drawn together by gravity.

questions.q: In a main sequence star, nuclear fusion joins together nuclei of which element?
questions.explain: Main sequence stars fuse hydrogen nuclei into helium, releasing energy.

questions.q: A star about the size of the Sun eventually shrinks to become a stable, dense:
questions.explain: After the red giant stage, a Sun-sized star collapses into a white dwarf.

questions.q: The huge explosion of a very massive star at the end of its life is called a:
questions.explain: A massive star explodes as a supernova after its red super giant stage.

questions.q: Red-shift is the shift of light from distant galaxies towards:
options: Longer wavelengths (the red end of the spectrum)
Shorter wavelengths (the blue end of the spectrum)
The gamma-ray end of the spectrum
questions.explain: Light from receding galaxies is stretched to longer wavelengths, shifting it towards red.

questions.q: Our Sun is one star among many billions in which galaxy?
questions.explain: The Sun is one of the many stars that make up the Milky Way galaxy.

questions.q: Why does a main sequence star remain stable in size for a long time?
options: The inward pull of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure from fusion
Gravity is switched off during this stage
There are no forces acting on the star
The star is not producing any energy
questions.explain: In a stable star, gravity pulling inwards is balanced by the outward pressure from nuclear fusion.

questions.q: The red-shift seen in light from distant galaxies is evidence that:
questions.explain: Red-shift shows galaxies are moving apart, indicating an expanding universe.

questions.q: Galaxies that are further away show a greater red-shift. This tells us that they are:
options: Moving away from us more slowly
questions.explain: Greater red-shift means a faster recession, so more distant galaxies move away faster.

questions.q: Elements heavier than iron are mainly formed:
questions.explain: Fusion in stars produces elements up to iron; heavier elements form in the extreme conditions of a supernova.

questions.q: A star much more massive than the Sun ends its life cycle as a:
options: Neutron star or a black hole
questions.explain: After a supernova, a very massive star's core forms either a neutron star or a black hole.

questions.q: Cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) is important because it provides evidence for:
options: The formation of the Solar System
questions.explain: CMBR is radiation left over from the early universe and supports the Big Bang theory.

questions.q: Compared with the near-circular orbits of the planets, comets travel around the Sun in orbits that are:
questions.explain: Comets follow very elongated, elliptical orbits that bring them close to and then far from the Sun.

questions.q: As a protostar contracts under gravity its temperature rises until it becomes hot enough for:
options: The star to cool and fade
questions.explain: Rising temperature and pressure eventually trigger nuclear fusion, forming a main sequence star.

questions.q: A newly formed star is about 20 times more massive than the Sun. Which sequence best predicts its life cycle?
options: Main sequence star to red super giant to supernova to black hole
Main sequence star to red giant to white dwarf to black dwarf
Nebula to white dwarf to supernova to neutron star
Red giant to supernova to nebula to main sequence star
questions.explain: Very massive stars swell into red super giants, explode as supernovae, then form a neutron star or black hole.

questions.q: Galaxy A shows a small red-shift and Galaxy B shows a large red-shift. Which statement is correct?
options: Galaxy B is further away and moving away faster
Galaxy A is further away and moving away faster
Galaxy B is moving towards us
questions.explain: A larger red-shift indicates a greater distance and a faster speed of recession.

questions.q: Which of these shows the correct order of stages in the life cycle of a star the size of the Sun?
options: Nebula to main sequence star to red giant to white dwarf
Main sequence star to nebula to red giant to white dwarf
Nebula to red giant to main sequence star to white dwarf
Red giant to nebula to white dwarf to main sequence star
questions.explain: A Sun-sized star forms from a nebula, becomes a main sequence star, swells to a red giant, then collapses to a white dwarf.

questions.q: An astronomer finds that light from every distant galaxy is red-shifted, and that more distant galaxies are red-shifted more. This best supports the idea that:
options: The whole universe is expanding from an initial Big Bang
The Solar System is at the centre of the universe
All galaxies are moving towards the Milky Way
The stars are running out of fuel
questions.explain: Universal red-shift increasing with distance is key evidence for an expanding universe and the Big Bang.
